data.content_ref: inline:The mechanism conflates two conceptually distinct Popperian properties—empirical content (degree of falsifiability, a logical/a priori feature of a theory's form) and corroboration (survival of severe tests, a historical/a posteriori fact)—treating them as equivalent via apposition: 'it has survived the most severe tests (highest empirical content).' These properties come apart: a newly proposed theory can have maximal empirical content yet minimal corroboration, while a long-standing theory can be well-corroborated yet have only moderate content. The mechanism's stated goal is to select 'the most informative target for the next attempt at falsification,' and informativeness is determined by content, not by past survival. But the target's claim is about preference for better-*corroborated* theories. If content drives the selection, the mechanism justifies preference for the highest-content theory, not the best-corroborated one, and the claim misidentifies what is being preferred. If corroboration (past survival) drives the selection, the mechanism relies on past performance as a basis for future-oriented choice—which is precisely the inductive inference the claim disavows. The mechanism cannot resolve this tension because it never distinguishes the two criteria, instead smuggling them together so the reader cannot tell whether the defense is trivial (choose high content) or inductive (choose what survived).
